summary: This document analyzes threats to telephone identity in the interconnected Internet and telephone network, where attackers can impersonate or hide calling numbers. It lists actors, their capabilities and the attacks, to guide the design of countermeasures.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7375 analyzes how callers can present telephone numbers they are not authorized to use. It describes the people and systems involved, the resulting attacks, and the scope of the threat.

subtitle: Threats involving impersonation of calling telephone numbers

tldr.problem: Call signaling can carry a calling number chosen by the caller, even when the caller is not authorized to use that number. This can support fraud, unwanted calls, and denial of service.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the scope, actors, attacker capabilities, attack types, and call-path scenarios that a secure telephone identity solution should consider.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7375 is a threat model for the Secure Telephone Identity work. It does not define a countermeasure or protocol.

facts.label: Identity in scope
facts.value: Calling telephone number at call setup

today: RFC 7375 is an Informational document and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It provides a threat model for the Secure Telephone Identity work, not a solution.

sections.title: What the Threat Model Covers
sections.content:
The document focuses on the calling telephone number shown to a person or automated service when a call is set up. It assumes that an attacker can create signaling with a chosen number, so the goal for future solutions is to help the receiving side distinguish authorized from unauthorized numbers.

The scope does not include impersonating a listener after a call starts, verifying the called party to the caller, changes made after call setup, or attacks aimed specifically at caller names. It also does not consider compromised intermediaries or operators deliberately falsifying identity.
sections.plainLanguage: The threat is a false calling number shown when a call begins. This RFC does not cover who receives the call or changes made after setup.

sections.title: Endpoints, Intermediaries, and Attackers
sections.content:
Endpoints include simple telephone devices, programmable devices such as smartphones or computers, and automated services such as voicemail. Intermediaries forward call signaling and may modify it. A gateway is an intermediary that translates signaling between protocols.

The threat model assumes that an attacker can place calls over the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN) or Internet Protocol (IP), supply any calling number, capture and replay signaling, and access the Internet. It does not assume that the attacker has compromised an intermediary or stolen credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: Calls may pass through phones, automated services, and systems that translate or change call signaling. The attacker can choose a calling number and replay signaling, but compromised network systems are outside this model.

sections.title: Attacks Enabled by Number Impersonation
sections.content:
Voicemail systems or other services may grant access based partly or entirely on the calling number. An attacker who presents the target's number may exploit that behavior. The RFC notes that a service could require another check, such as a PIN, when calling-number information is not authenticated.

Robocallers can present plausible or unassigned numbers to disguise their identity. Telephony denial-of-service attacks use repeated calls to make a target number hard to reach; changing or impersonating numbers can make simple blocking harder. Authenticated calling-number information may support policy decisions, but the RFC says it is unlikely to solve attacks against emergency responders who must try to answer every call.
sections.plainLanguage: A false number can fool services that trust caller numbers and can hide the source of unwanted calls. Number checks may help, but the RFC does not claim they stop every attack.

sections.title: How a Chosen Number Reaches the Receiver
sections.content:
The RFC describes four call paths: IP to IP, PSTN to PSTN, IP to PSTN, and IP to PSTN to IP. In the IP-to-IP example, the attacker puts the chosen number in the SIP INVITE's From field. In a PSTN path, a private branch exchange may put it in a Q.931 setup message, which a provider carries into SS7 signaling.

Gateways can translate the calling number between protocols and carry it toward the terminating telephone system. The RFC leaves attacks specific to future in-band and out-of-band solutions for later analysis, while listing replay, message removal, false stored data, and attacks on directories as issues to consider.
sections.plainLanguage: The call may travel entirely over IP, entirely over the phone network, or through both. In each case, signaling can carry the attacker's chosen number to the receiver.

sections.title: Limits of the Threat Model
sections.content:
The RFC's Security Considerations section says that the document is a threat model and is therefore about security. Its analysis assumes the current problem is the lack of secure identity in call-signaling mechanisms.

The model does not treat an intermediary operator who intentionally discards valid identity information or sends false identity as an attacker. The RFC also notes that any countermeasure depends on secure design and operation of the systems that carry it.
sections.plainLanguage: This document catalogs threats rather than prescribing a defense. It assumes ordinary call intermediaries may change signaling, but not that their operators are attackers.
